Title 6: Review disposition codes in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management
Description:
Disposition codes define how returned products are handled after receipt and inspection. Each code combines a recognizable return disposition with an action, optional handling for component parts, and an optional quality-association check so returns follow consistent inventory and quality policy.

Create a unique code and description for each supported outcome and select the action that matches the organization’s return process. Where relevant, identify the disposition for component parts and determine whether a quality association must be checked. Align the design with warehouse, quality, inventory, customer service, and finance owners, and avoid codes whose names do not clearly communicate the resulting treatment.

Disposition codes are selected during customer-return processing and influence what happens to the returned quantity, including its inventory and quality path. Validate each code with a representative return through receipt and disposition, confirming the intended action, quality behavior, and downstream inventory result. Review codes when return policy, quality controls, repair practices, or warehouse processes change, because a wrong selection can make stock available incorrectly or route it to the wrong outcome.

Description:
The term plan to produce is used to describe a collection of business processes
that an organization implements to support the planning and execution of the
production process. Planning refers to the definition of production strategies,
reviewing the long-term production plan, and building a production schedule. The
production business process incorporates the activities before, during, and
after the execution of the procedures that result from taking raw materials and
creating sub-assemblies or finished goods.




The plan to produce process covers several different approaches to
manufacturing. For example, discrete manufacturing, process or batch
manufacturing, lean manufacturing, and job-shop manufacturing. These are all
considered different modes of manufacturing, but the core concepts in the
business process are largely the same.



The plan to produce process is highly interconnected to the other end to end
business processes, such as forecast to plan, procure to pay, inventory to
deliver, record to report, order to cash, and acquire to dispose. The upstream
or downstream relationship of plan to produce to the other processes is highly
dependent on the operational strategies of each organization. For example, plan
to produce could be an upstream process of order to cash in a make-to-stock
scenario, but would be a downstream process instead in a make to order scenario.
Organizations also often use multiple different operational strategies when they
offer different types of products. This choice is fully supported by Dynamics
365.



Note: It is important to note that the inventory management processes related to
plan to produce are not included in this process definition. They are located in
the inventory to deliver process. Learn more at Inventory to deliver -
introduction to the end-to-end business process.


Note: It is important to note that the supply and demand planning process is
part of the forecast to plan business process, and the planning in the plan to
produce process begins with scheduling production. Learn more at Forecast to
plan introduction.


The high-level strategy for plan to produce processes should be planned at the
early phases of a larger business solution. The design and decisions made about
this process have an impact on downstream processes including integrations, data
that must be migrated, and so on. The production process is often considered
business-critical scope for implementing a technology solution, but may
sometimes be slated for later phases when a finance-first implementation
strategy is chosen.



Every organization has variations to the plan to produce process. Here, we
define the basic outline for any organization looking to implement a Microsoft
technology solution to support the plan to produce process.

inspections, manual order closure) and plan for automation in Dynamics 365
finance and operations apps to improve visibility and reduce delays. * Use
Dynamics 365 finance and operations apps to visualize and analyze the entire
value stream, supporting process corrections and continuous improvement as
discussed.

responding to capital projects or internal requests. The process also supports
the integration of resource constraints, lead times, and prioritization rules,
enabling planners to balance efficiency with responsiveness.

transitioning a planned or scheduled production order from the planning phase
into active execution on the shop floor. This process starts when a production

prepared and provided to the production team. The release triggers procurement
of any required raw materials not already in stock, and ensures that all
relevant information—such as shop drawings, specifications, and instructions—is
communicated to the appropriate supervisors or workers. In practice, this step
formalizes the start of manufacturing activities, allowing workers to begin
assembling, fabricating, or processing items according to the order’s
requirements. The process also establishes accountability for tracking progress,
managing inventory consumption, and updating order status as work proceeds. By
releasing production to the shop floor, organizations ensure that production
activities are coordinated, resources are allocated efficiently, and the
transition from planning to execution is clearly documented, supporting accurate
reporting, cost tracking, and timely fulfillment of customer or internal orders.

Description:
The run production operations business process area covers the activities in an
organization's internal production process. Any manufacturing organization finds
it critical to track and control production operations. The goal is to ensure
consistent product quality and minimize production costs. Running production
operations also requires coordination and communication between many
departments, such as engineering, operations, quality, sales, planning, and
procurement.




The process for executing production operations varies from business to
business, depending on industry and product, but it follows the same basic
steps. At the beginning of production, materials are consumed into the process.
A combination of people and tools or machines then run the specific production
steps. Finally, the sub-assembly or finished good is created as the output of
the process. The definition of these steps is done as part of the Design to
retire end-to-end business processes and refined further in the define
production strategies business process area.



Define this business process at the beginning of an implementation of Dynamics
365 Supply Chain Management. It's a foundational process for any manufacturing
company.

implementation scope. It's also important to recognize that these processes are

industry. In that case, integrations to such systems may be required as part of
the Dynamics 365 implementation.

Description:
The source (previously procure to pay process, also known as purchase to pay) is
a term used to describe the entire process of purchasing goods or services from
a supplier and paying for them. The process includes all the steps from the
initial procurement request to the final payment to the supplier.



The procure to pay process typically includes the following steps:



 1. Identify the need for goods or services: This process covers both indirect
    procurement, where the goods or services are not related to the good or
    service being sold, and direct procurement, where demand for the goods or
    services exists within the production or sales processes. Dynamics 365
    Supply Chain Management supports flexible procurement processes based on
    business needs. These processes include request for quotations (RFQs),
    purchase requisitions, contracts (purchase agreements or blanket orders),
    and purchase orders which can be planned or unplanned. Planned purchase
    orders can be generated automatically from supply or demand forecasts
    present. Learn more at Forecast to plan introduction.
 2. Supplier selection: The procurement team evaluates potential suppliers and
    selects the one that meets the requirements. Dynamics 365 also includes
    functionality to help automate the supplier selection and portal
    capabilities to allow suppliers to apply online or even respond to requests
    for quotations.
 3. Purchase order creation: A purchase order is created and sent to the
    supplier. It specifies the goods or services required, the price, delivery
    date, and other terms and conditions. With Dynamics 365, the process may
    include a purchase requisition, purchase agreement (also known as a contract
    or blanket order), or a request for quotation.
 4. Invoice receipt and verification: The supplier sends an invoice for the
    goods or services, and the invoice is checked for accuracy and completeness.
    Dynamics 365 includes full AP automation capabilities with OCR through Azure
    Form Recognizer to assist with this process.
 5. Invoice approval: The invoice is approved for payment, and the accounts
    payable team processes the payment.
 6. Payment: The supplier is paid for the goods or services, usually by
    electronic funds transfer.
 7. Record keeping: All relevant documents, including the purchase order,
    invoice, and payment details, are recorded and stored for future reference.
 8. Reporting: Financial and operational report analysis help keep track of
    performance of the procure to pay process. You can include supply risk
    analysis, purchase order backorders, vendor performance, and spend analysis.



The procure to pay process is a crucial aspect of business operations, and
efficient execution can result in cost savings, increased transparency, and
better supplier relationships.



Important: The process defined here does not include the goods receipt process.
Learn more at Inventory to deliver.


Every organization has variations to procure to pay. Here, we define the basic
outline for any organization looking to implement a technology solution to
support the procure to pay process.

that are needed within your organization. During this process, the sourcing or

time as your business and operations change and evolve to support your

procurement and sourcing strategies to ensure you're receiving the best pricing,
lead time, and quality for your products and services.

Description:
Develop procurement catalogs establishes a governed, user-friendly buying
experience by organizing approved goods and services into internal catalogs,
connecting to supplier webstores via punchout, enabling vendor self‑service
contributions, and importing supplier product lists to keep content current and
compliant.

Scope and intended outcomes
This process standardizes how employees discover items during requisitioning,
ensures negotiated prices and terms are applied, shortens cycle time, and
improves spend compliance. It spans catalog strategy and hierarchy design,
internal catalog curation, external punchout enablement (cXML/OCI), vendor
self‑service contributions through a portal, and scheduled imports to refresh
products and prices.

Core concepts to anchor the design

 * Procurement catalogs can expose stock and non‑stock items or category-only
   lines for services; a category hierarchy supports both itemized and
   non‑itemized purchasing, and is typically defined early in the ERP program so
   downstream requisition and PO flows align. 
 * External (punchout) catalogs let requesters shop on a supplier’s site and
   return a validated cart to your requisition, commonly via cXML; this avoids
   duplicating large assortments while keeping approvals and accounting in your
   system of record. 
 * Vendor self‑service (supplier collaboration portal) reduces buyer workload by
   letting vendors maintain item attributes, confirmations, and price lists
   within governance boundaries. 
 * Vendor catalog import brings supplier items, pricing, and attributes into
   your internal catalogs using governed templates and mappings, ensuring
   searchability and price accuracy at scale. 

Catalog types you’ll typically combine

 * Internal procurement catalogs: curated lists of items/services with
   categories, attributes, UOM, approved vendors, and trade/agreement pricing;
   ideal for frequently purchased goods and internal service menus. 
 * External punchout catalogs: supplier-hosted assortments accessed from your
   requisitioning UI; appropriate when assortments change frequently or are too
   large to maintain internally. 
 * Hybrid catalogs: internal for core SKUs plus punchout for long tails and
   specialized categories (e.g., MRO, IT accessories). 

Governance decisions and data model
Define the procurement category hierarchy (depth, naming, coding), mandatory
attributes, and approval policies by category. Establish catalog ownership
(Category Manager, Buyer), SLAs for updates, and quality rules for item data
(images, tax attributes, UNSPSC, substitutes). Align security so employees see
only catalogs relevant to their role, region, cost center, and contract
entitlements. 
Plan import formats and validations (e.g., cXML, CSV) and map supplier
attributes to your canonical schema to support search facets and analytical
rollups. 

Integration and experience design

 * Requisition experience: employees browse catalogs filtered by policy;
   accounting is derived via category mapping and budgets can be checked before
   approval. 
 * Punchout: configure the supplier connection, authentication, and return cart
   mapping; decide which categories route to punchout versus internal items. 
 * Vendor self‑service: enable selected suppliers to propose items or maintain
   pricing via the collaboration portal under workflow and audit. 

High - level process

 1.  Assess scope and policies: confirm which categories and suppliers will be
     catalog‑driven, which will use punchout, and which will remain free‑text or
     RFQ‑led; confirm approval thresholds and budget rules. 
 2.  Design the catalog hierarchy: define category tree, attribute sets, and
     required data for items and services (including non‑itemized service
     categories) to support requisitioning and analytics. 
 3.  Configure internal catalogs: create catalogs, assign products and
     categories, attach price/trade agreements, and set visibility/security for
     requester groups. 
 4.  Enable punchout suppliers: establish external catalog connections (e.g.,
     cXML), map categories to the supplier’s scope, and test round‑trip cart and
     accounting defaults. 
 5.  Set up vendor self‑service: grant portal access, define what vendors can
     maintain (prices, lead times, substitutions), and route changes through
     workflow with audit. 
 6.  Import vendor products: agree on file formats and cadence; validate content
     against your schema; load items and prices; link to catalogs and
     categories; log exceptions for supplier remediation. 
 7.  Pilot and refine: run a pilot with key requesters and suppliers; measure
     findability, price coverage, and approval cycle time; adjust hierarchy,
     attributes, and visibility. 
 8.  Launch with guided buying: publish catalogs, provide “how‑to” tips in the
     requisition workspace, and communicate when to use internal vs. punchout. 
 9.  Operate and refresh: monitor price accuracy, broken links, and stale items;
     schedule vendor catalog imports; audit portal changes; retire duplicate or
     low‑use content. 
 10. Expand coverage: add categories and new punchout partners; introduce
     supplier-managed content for fast‑moving categories under tighter
     guardrails. 

Roles and responsibilities

 * Procurement Category Manager: owns hierarchy, curation standards, and catalog
   roadmap; approves supplier‑submitted changes. 
 * Buyer/Procurement Operations: configures catalogs, manages imports, resolves
   data exceptions, and monitors punchout uptime. 
 * Supplier (via portal): maintains agreed product and price data; responds to
   content quality feedback; complies with update schedules. 
 * Requester: follows catalog policies; uses approved catalogs or punchout;
   avoids free‑text when catalog coverage exists. 

Dynamics 365 product support

 * Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management provides procurement category
   hierarchies, internal catalog setup, purchasing policies, and the supplier
   collaboration portal; it supports punchout catalogs and mapping of external
   carts back to requisitions.
 * Vendor catalog import capabilities let you bring in supplier items and prices
   and attach them to your catalogs with governed templates. 
 * Source‑to‑pay solution guidance highlights “Punch‑out catalogs” and “Vendor
   collaboration portal” in the standard capability map, confirming fit within
   the L2/L3 process model. 

Operational controls and KPIs
Institute change workflows, reason codes, and periodic reviews; segregate duties
between content authors and approvers. Track: catalog coverage (% of spend via
catalogs), punchout success rate, search-to-add time, price variance vs.
contract, stale item rate, and supplier content SLA adherence.

Title 5: Create external punch out catalogs in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management
Description:
External punch out catalogs in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management allow
organizations to connect directly to supplier-hosted catalogs via standard
protocols (e.g., cXML, OCI). Users can "punch out" from Dynamics 365 to the
supplier's website, select items, and return the shopping cart to Dynamics 365
for requisition and approval. This approach ensures real-time access to supplier
offerings, negotiated pricing, and up-to-date product information, while
maintaining control over the procurement process within Dynamics 365. Punch out
catalogs support seamless integration with supplier e-commerce platforms,
automating data exchange and reducing manual entry errors.

suppliers to manage and update their own catalog offerings via a secure portal.

subject to buyer review and approval. This self-service model reduces
administrative overhead, improves data accuracy, and accelerates the onboarding
of new items. The portal supports workflow-driven approvals, compliance checks,
and integration with procurement processes, ensuring that only validated items
are available for requisition.

Description:
Develop supplier segments organizes the vendor base into meaningful groups so
procurement can target sourcing strategies, enforce policies, track supplier
diversity, and optimize buying outcomes across categories, regions, and business
units.

This process supports both portal-driven segmentation (via supplier
collaboration) and manual maintenance in the ERP, and it explicitly includes
supplier diversity attributes and purchasing demographics.

Scope and outcomes The process defines the segmentation framework, enriches
suppliers with the attributes that place them into segments, and keeps those
segments current as suppliers onboard, update certifications, or performance
shifts. Outcomes include clear segment definitions (e.g., strategic vs.
transactional), validated diversity classifications, visibility into purchasing
demographics (who buys from whom, where, and for what), and segment-specific
playbooks for sourcing, risk, and performance management.

Segmentation model (what to capture)

 * Business identity: legal entity, parent/child relationships, tax IDs,
   NAICS/industry, geography.
 * Commercial markers: category fit, price lists/trade agreements, contract
   status, capacity/lead times, delivery lanes.
 * Risk and compliance: sanctions/KYC status, insurance, sustainability/ESG
   attestations, cybersecurity posture.
 * Performance: on‑time delivery, quality metrics, responsiveness, dispute rate,
   claim history.
 * Diversity: minority‑owned, women‑owned, veteran‑owned, disability‑owned,
   LGBTQ+‑owned, small/disadvantaged business, indigenous, local/regional
   designations; certification bodies; effective/expiry dates.
 * Purchasing demographics: spend by business unit/region/cost center, category
   mix, order frequency, average PO value, tail vs. strategic spend share.

Data sources (how it gets populated)

 * Supplier collaboration portal self‑service forms for profile, certifications,
   banking, sustainability and diversity disclosures, with evidence uploads and
   dates.
 * Manual entry in system for vendor groups, classifications, category
   assignments, and policy flags when portal is not in scope.
 * Controlled imports (CSV/cXML/API) from supplier registries (e.g., diversity
   certifiers), CLM systems, and performance data from receiving/quality
   modules.

Operating model

 * Portal‑driven segmentation: suppliers submit/maintain profile and
   certifications; workflows validate and place suppliers into segments
   automatically based on rules.
 * Manual in‑system segmentation: procurement analysts assign vendor groups,
   risk scores, diversity flags, and category memberships directly in ERP when
   collaboration is unavailable or during transition.
 * Hybrid: start manual to establish baseline, then transition segments to
   portal upkeep; keep critical attributes under workflow (e.g., bank changes,
   diversity certification).

High‑level process

 1.  Define segment taxonomy and rules
     
     * Set the canonical list of segments (e.g., strategic, preferred,
       qualified, tail), diversity attributes, and risk tiers; publish the
       decision rules and data dictionary.

 2.  Configure master data and security
     
     * Create vendor groups/classes, category associations, mandatory
       attributes, and approval workflows. Set role‑based access for who can
       view/change sensitive fields.

 3.  Enable the supplier collaboration portal
     
     * Publish onboarding questionnaires, required documents, and self‑service
       profile pages for diversity, sustainability, and banking; map each field
       to ERP attributes.

 4.  Collect and validate data
     
     * Intake portal submissions and imports; validate certifications (issuer,
       number, effective/expiry), run basic KYC/sanctions checks, and flag
       missing or expired evidence.

 5.  Apply segmentation rules
     
     * Assign segment, risk tier, and diversity status based on rules (e.g.,
       spend thresholds, category fit, performance, certifications). Record
       effective dates and rationale.

 6.  Enrich with purchasing demographics
     
     * Link historic and rolling spend by BU/region/category to the supplier
       record; compute purchase frequency, order size, and tail‑spend indicators
       to refine segment placement.

 7.  Approve and publish segments
     
     * Route changes through workflow for procurement/category manager approval;
       publish segments to sourcing, requisitioning policies, and supplier
       performance dashboards.

 8.  Govern usage in downstream processes
     
     * Bind segments to policies (e.g., RFQ routing to “preferred,” auto‑blocks
       for “not qualified,” diversity‑spend targets in analytics, guided buying
       recommendations).

 9.  Monitor and refresh
     
     * Schedule reviews for expiring certifications, material performance
       shifts, M&A events; automatically notify suppliers via portal to update
       expiring documents.

 10. Improve the model
     
     * Review segment drift vs. outcomes (savings, risk incidents,
       diversity‑spend attainment); refine rules and thresholds; retire unused
       attributes.

Roles and responsibilities

 * Procurement/category manager: owns taxonomy, thresholds, and approvals;
   resolves exceptions.
 * Supplier onboarding/operations: validates submissions, runs checks, and
   manages workflows.
 * Diversity & inclusion lead (or ESG): defines accepted certification bodies
   and target reporting.
 * Risk/compliance: maintains KYC/sanctions rules, approves sensitive changes.
 * Finance/AP: verifies banking and tax data; ensures SoD and auditability.
 * Business stakeholders: supply purchasing demographics and feedback on
   supplier fit.

Dynamics 365 support

 * Vendor information management and vendor groups/classifications for segments,
   risk, and policies.
 * Supplier collaboration portal for self‑service profile maintenance,
   confirmations, and document upload.
 * Purchasing policies that reference vendor groups/segments to allow/deny
   categories or enforce RFQs.
 * Trade agreements and approved vendor list to bind segments to price/contract
   usage.
 * Analytics via Power BI/Microsoft Fabric to report diversity spend, segment
   performance, tail spend, and purchasing demographics.

Supplier diversity and purchasing demographics (practical guidance)

 * Diversity capture: model diversity as structured fields with certification
   authority, certificate ID, effective/expiry, and attach artifacts;
   differentiate self‑attested vs. certified.
 * Targets and tracking: define percentage goals (e.g., percent of addressable
   spend to certified diverse suppliers) by category and region; monitor
   progress monthly.
 * Purchasing demographics: publish a quarterly heatmap showing who buys from
   which segments by business unit and location; use it to rebalance work to
   diverse/preferred suppliers without increasing risk.
 * Guardrails: enforce evidence-on-file rules for diversity claims and
   auto‑expire designations upon certificate expiry; route reinstatement through
   validation workflow.

Operational controls and KPIs

 * Controls: maker‑checker for profile changes; workflowed approvals for
   risk/diversity flags; automated reminders for expiring certifications; audit
   trails for attribute changes.
 * KPIs: percent of spend through preferred/strategic segments; diverse‑supplier
   spend attainment; number of active diverse suppliers by category/region;
   average time to validate new supplier; share of tail spend; policy violations
   avoided; data completeness score for vendor profiles.

Deliverables

 * Segmentation taxonomy and data dictionary.
 * Configured vendor groups/classifications and workflows.
 * Onboarding questionnaires and document lists (portal).
 * Diversity certification playbook and accepted issuers list.
 * Dashboards: diversity spend, purchasing demographics, segment performance.

Description:
Develop supplier segments organizes the vendor base into meaningful groups so
procurement can target sourcing strategies, enforce policies, track supplier
diversity, and optimize buying outcomes across categories, regions, and business
units.

This process supports both portal-driven segmentation (via supplier
collaboration) and manual maintenance in the ERP, and it explicitly includes
supplier diversity attributes and purchasing demographics.

Scope and outcomes The process defines the segmentation framework, enriches
suppliers with the attributes that place them into segments, and keeps those
segments current as suppliers onboard, update certifications, or performance
shifts. Outcomes include clear segment definitions (e.g., strategic vs.
transactional), validated diversity classifications, visibility into purchasing
demographics (who buys from whom, where, and for what), and segment-specific
playbooks for sourcing, risk, and performance management.

Segmentation model (what to capture)

 * Business identity: legal entity, parent/child relationships, tax IDs,
   NAICS/industry, geography.
 * Commercial markers: category fit, price lists/trade agreements, contract
   status, capacity/lead times, delivery lanes.
 * Risk and compliance: sanctions/KYC status, insurance, sustainability/ESG
   attestations, cybersecurity posture.
 * Performance: on‑time delivery, quality metrics, responsiveness, dispute rate,
   claim history.
 * Diversity: minority‑owned, women‑owned, veteran‑owned, disability‑owned,
   LGBTQ+‑owned, small/disadvantaged business, indigenous, local/regional
   designations; certification bodies; effective/expiry dates.
 * Purchasing demographics: spend by business unit/region/cost center, category
   mix, order frequency, average PO value, tail vs. strategic spend share.

Data sources (how it gets populated)

 * Supplier collaboration portal self‑service forms for profile, certifications,
   banking, sustainability and diversity disclosures, with evidence uploads and
   dates.
 * Manual entry in system for vendor groups, classifications, category
   assignments, and policy flags when portal is not in scope.
 * Controlled imports (CSV/cXML/API) from supplier registries (e.g., diversity
   certifiers), CLM systems, and performance data from receiving/quality
   modules.

Operating model

 * Portal‑driven segmentation: suppliers submit/maintain profile and
   certifications; workflows validate and place suppliers into segments
   automatically based on rules.
 * Manual in‑system segmentation: procurement analysts assign vendor groups,
   risk scores, diversity flags, and category memberships directly in ERP when
   collaboration is unavailable or during transition.
 * Hybrid: start manual to establish baseline, then transition segments to
   portal upkeep; keep critical attributes under workflow (e.g., bank changes,
   diversity certification).

High‑level process

 1.  Define segment taxonomy and rules
     
     * Set the canonical list of segments (e.g., strategic, preferred,
       qualified, tail), diversity attributes, and risk tiers; publish the
       decision rules and data dictionary.

 2.  Configure master data and security
     
     * Create vendor groups/classes, category associations, mandatory
       attributes, and approval workflows. Set role‑based access for who can
       view/change sensitive fields.

 3.  Enable the supplier collaboration portal
     
     * Publish onboarding questionnaires, required documents, and self‑service
       profile pages for diversity, sustainability, and banking; map each field
       to ERP attributes.

 4.  Collect and validate data
     
     * Intake portal submissions and imports; validate certifications (issuer,
       number, effective/expiry), run basic KYC/sanctions checks, and flag
       missing or expired evidence.

 5.  Apply segmentation rules
     
     * Assign segment, risk tier, and diversity status based on rules (e.g.,
       spend thresholds, category fit, performance, certifications). Record
       effective dates and rationale.

 6.  Enrich with purchasing demographics
     
     * Link historic and rolling spend by BU/region/category to the supplier
       record; compute purchase frequency, order size, and tail‑spend indicators
       to refine segment placement.

 7.  Approve and publish segments
     
     * Route changes through workflow for procurement/category manager approval;
       publish segments to sourcing, requisitioning policies, and supplier
       performance dashboards.

 8.  Govern usage in downstream processes
     
     * Bind segments to policies (e.g., RFQ routing to “preferred,” auto‑blocks
       for “not qualified,” diversity‑spend targets in analytics, guided buying
       recommendations).

 9.  Monitor and refresh
     
     * Schedule reviews for expiring certifications, material performance
       shifts, M&A events; automatically notify suppliers via portal to update
       expiring documents.

 10. Improve the model
     
     * Review segment drift vs. outcomes (savings, risk incidents,
       diversity‑spend attainment); refine rules and thresholds; retire unused
       attributes.

Roles and responsibilities

 * Procurement/category manager: owns taxonomy, thresholds, and approvals;
   resolves exceptions.
 * Supplier onboarding/operations: validates submissions, runs checks, and
   manages workflows.
 * Diversity & inclusion lead (or ESG): defines accepted certification bodies
   and target reporting.
 * Risk/compliance: maintains KYC/sanctions rules, approves sensitive changes.
 * Finance/AP: verifies banking and tax data; ensures SoD and auditability.
 * Business stakeholders: supply purchasing demographics and feedback on
   supplier fit.

Dynamics 365 support

 * Vendor information management and vendor groups/classifications for segments,
   risk, and policies.
 * Supplier collaboration portal for self‑service profile maintenance,
   confirmations, and document upload.
 * Purchasing policies that reference vendor groups/segments to allow/deny
   categories or enforce RFQs.
 * Trade agreements and approved vendor list to bind segments to price/contract
   usage.
 * Analytics via Power BI/Microsoft Fabric to report diversity spend, segment
   performance, tail spend, and purchasing demographics.

Supplier diversity and purchasing demographics (practical guidance)

 * Diversity capture: model diversity as structured fields with certification
   authority, certificate ID, effective/expiry, and attach artifacts;
   differentiate self‑attested vs. certified.
 * Targets and tracking: define percentage goals (e.g., percent of addressable
   spend to certified diverse suppliers) by category and region; monitor
   progress monthly.
 * Purchasing demographics: publish a quarterly heatmap showing who buys from
   which segments by business unit and location; use it to rebalance work to
   diverse/preferred suppliers without increasing risk.
 * Guardrails: enforce evidence-on-file rules for diversity claims and
   auto‑expire designations upon certificate expiry; route reinstatement through
   validation workflow.

Operational controls and KPIs

 * Controls: maker‑checker for profile changes; workflow approvals for
   risk/diversity flags; automated reminders for expiring certifications; audit
   trails for attribute changes.
 * KPIs: percent of spend through preferred/strategic segments; diverse‑supplier
   spend attainment; number of active diverse suppliers by category/region;
   average time to validate new supplier; share of tail spend; policy violations
   avoided; data completeness score for vendor profiles.

Deliverables

 * Segmentation taxonomy and data dictionary.
 * Configured vendor groups/classifications and workflows.
 * Onboarding questionnaires and document lists (portal).
 * Diversity certification playbook and accepted issuers list.
 * Dashboards: diversity spend, purchasing demographics, segment performance.

Description:
Define accounts payable policies establishes a single, governed rulebook for how
your organization receives, validates, approves, pays, and accounts for supplier
invoices—covering invoice matching, exceptions, cash discounts, payment methods,
prepayments, rebates/allowances, and audit controls so AP is fast, compliant,
and predictable.

Scope and objectives

 * Standardize AP across legal entities for invoicing, payments, cash
   discounting, prepayments, supplier rebates/allowances, and exceptions, with
   clear approval matrices and segregation of duties (SoD).
 * Encode policies as system behavior (workflows, tolerances, holds, and
   validations) in Dynamics 365 Finance to reduce cycle time and errors.

Invoicing policies

 * Invoice intake channels and requirements: define accepted channels
   (EDI/PEPPOL, vendor portal, email/OCR), mandatory header/line data, tax/VAT
   rules, and duplicate detection. In Dynamics 365 Finance, use invoice matching
   (two‑way/three‑way/totals) with variance tolerances; breaches route to
   workflow before posting.
 * Matching and tolerances: set price/quantity/total thresholds by category or
   vendor; use three‑way matching where receiving is required; log and resolve
   discrepancies before posting.
 * Non‑PO invoice policy: strictly limit categories that may bypass matching;
   enforce specialty approval and SoD; document required supporting evidence.
 * Dispute management: define timelines and roles to resolve price/quantity
   defects and short‑shipments; hold invoices from payment until resolved.

Payment policies

 * Payment run cadence and proposal rules: standardize weekly/biweekly runs
   using payment proposals (due‑date and cash‑discount date logic) with
   review/approval checkpoints.
 * Methods of payment: permit ACH/wire/promissory notes; define positive pay and
   file formats; restrict checks and mandate treasury review for new
   methods/partners. Configure Positive Pay and payment types/fees in AP.
 * Centralized payments and cross‑company: enable centralized AP where
   appropriate; set bank validation and reversal policies; log approvals for
   manual wires.
 * Single Payment Requests (ad hoc): prohibit use when a PO is required; enforce
   privacy/SSPA and anti‑corruption controls; require controller approval for
   prepayments.

Cash discounting policies

 * Terms and calculations: define standard terms, discount bases (tax
   included/excluded), and treatment of under/over‑payments; permit “outside
   window” discounts only under defined approvals. Configure “cash discount is
   calculated including tax” and cash‑discount administration settings.
 * Payment selection: use payment proposals to prioritize invoices by discount
   date, then due date.

Prepayments and advances

 * Distinguish prepayment invoices vs. prepayments; require controller approval,
   proof‑of‑execution after service, and recovery for undelivered goods—no
   “parking of funds.” 

Supplier rebates and trade allowances

 * Define eligibility, accrual method, required evidence, approval flow, and
   settlement cadence; align AP handling with procurement contracts/rebate
   programs. 

Data governance, risk, and compliance

 * Vendor master controls: workflow for vendor creation and bank changes,
   SSPA/privacy prerequisites, sanctions screening, and diversity
   classifications where required.
 * SoD and auditability: dual control for bank edits and payments over
   threshold; versioned policy repository; retention and traceable approvals
   (MSApprovals).

KPIs and guardrails

 * First‑pass match rate; invoice exception rate; average days to approve;
   on‑time payment rate; cash discount captured vs. lost; positive pay
   exceptions; duplicate‑invoice prevention rate; prepayment recovery rate. 

High - level process 1) Define policy framework and decision rights (owners,
SoD, approval matrices). Publish a versioned AP Policy Handbook and change
process. 
2) Translate policies into system controls: configure matching
methods/tolerances, required fields, workflows, and holds in AP.
3) Set payment governance: payment proposal criteria, payment methods, positive
pay, centralized payments, and reversal rules. 
4) Establish cash‑discount rules and selection logic; align treasury calendars
to capture discounts. 
5) Define prepayment controls and documentation (controller approvals, POE
collection, recovery rules).
6) Codify non‑PO invoice exceptions and specialty categories; enforce workflows
and documentation.
7) Implement vendor governance: onboarding, bank validation workflows,
SSPA/privacy sanctions checks.
8) Roll out training, supplier guides (invoicing requirements, e‑invoice/EDI
specs, positive pay remittance details).
9) Monitor and improve: track KPIs, audit exceptions, and refine thresholds; run
quarterly policy reviews.

Roles and responsibilities

 * AP Manager: owns daily operations, exception queues, and KPI reporting;
   maintains matching and tolerance policies. 
 * Controller: owns approval matrices, prepayment and non‑PO exception
   governance, and audit readiness. 
 * Treasury: owns payment methods, bank relationships, positive pay, and wire
   approvals.
 * Procurement: aligns invoice requirements to contracts, vendor terms, and
   rebates; ensures PO integrity and change‑management workflows.
 * Risk/Compliance: monitors SoD, sanctions/privacy adherence, and policy
   enforcement.

Dynamics 365 configuration pointers

 * Accounts payable home: vendor payment setup (methods, fees, terms); positive
   pay; payment proposals; centralized payments; reversals.
 * Invoice matching: define totals/two‑way/three‑way matching with variance
   icons and tolerance thresholds; block posting outside tolerance.
 * Payment proposals: select by due date or cash‑discount date; schedule and
   review prior to posting.
 * Cash discounts: configure discount codes/series, tax‑inclusive calculation,
   and under/over‑payment handling.

Deliverables

 * AP Policy Handbook (version‑controlled) and Approval/Signing Limit Matrix;
   Supplier Invoicing Guide; Payment Methods Playbook; Prepayment & POE
   Checklist; Matching & Tolerance Matrix; KPIs dashboard (Power BI).

how and when supplier payments are processed. This includes establishing payment
terms (e.g., net 30), payment methods (ACH, check, wire), approval requirements,
batch processing schedules, and compliance with regulatory and audit controls.

segregation of duties, and integration with banking platforms. Payment policies
also cover exception handling for failed payments, manual payments, and
recurring payments. The objective is to ensure timely, accurate, and secure
disbursement of funds, minimize risk, and maintain auditability.

Description:
Develop spend strategy aligns procurement budgets to business goals, enforces
budget control and signing limits, and governs in‑year budget transfers so
sourcing and purchasing decisions stay compliant, timely, and cost‑effective.

Scope and objectives
This process defines how procurement dollars are planned, approved, and steered
across categories, business units, and regions. It codifies the rules for budget
authoring and phasing, budget control checks during requisition and purchase
order creation, monetary approval thresholds (signing limits), and the mechanics
for budget transfers and amendments. Outcomes include predictable spend, higher
budget adherence, fewer last‑minute waivers, and faster approvals without
sacrificing control.

Core policy levers

 * Budget ownership and structure: Define who owns category and cost‑center
   budgets; align to fiscal calendar, entities, and dimensions (business unit,
   region, category).
 * Spend guardrails: Set signing limits by role, risk, and category; require
   competitive sourcing or RFQ above thresholds; define change‑order time
   fences.
 * Control mode: Choose hard‑stop (block over‑budget) vs. soft‑warning (allow
   with justification) with consistent exception handling and audit.
 * Transfers and amendments: Permit controlled in‑year moves across cost
   centers/categories, with pre‑set caps, justification, and approvals.
 * Cash discounting and payment timing: Encourage early‑pay where economics are
   favorable and within cash/working‑capital targets.
 * Diversity and sustainability aims: Reserve portions of category budgets or
   set targets that influence award decisions without breaching policy.

Budgeting model (planning and phasing)
Start with a top‑down target by category and business unit, refine bottom‑up
with forecast demand (projects, run‑rate, seasonality), and phase monthly or
quarterly. Map contract commitments and blanket POs to budgets, and separate
controllable OpEx vs. pass‑throughs. Maintain a controlled “contingency” slice
for urgent/unplanned demand.

Budget control at point of spend
Enable budget checks at requisition, purchase order confirmation, and change
order. Controls should evaluate the correct accounting dimensions, recognize
pre‑encumbrance/encumbrance where used, and consider open commitments. Define
tolerances (for price variances, freight, taxes) and what triggers a re‑approval
vs. warning. For centrally negotiated contracts, reserve capacity to reduce
approval churn.

Signing limits and approvals
Publish a single signing‑limit matrix that considers amount, risk (e.g.,
non‑standard terms), and category. Drive approvals from category and monetary
thresholds, not individual preferences. Require dual approval for high‑risk
items (e.g., prepayments, new vendor, non‑PO spend). Enforce Segregation of
Duties so requesters cannot approve their own spend or vendor master/bank
changes.

Budget transfers and in‑year adjustments
Allow controlled transfers between cost centers/categories with:

 * Clear reasons (demand shift, price change, project acceleration).
 * Caps (e.g., ≤10% of original budget without CFO OK).
 * Traceable journal entries, effective dates, and audit trails.
 * A quarterly rebasing cadence to avoid constant micro‑moves.
   Emergency top‑ups should be routed via a short, documented approval path with
   post‑facto review.

Change‑order and variance governance
Define which changes (quantity, price, schedule) require re‑approval and which
can be auto‑accepted within tolerances. Log root causes (scope change, supplier
lead time, FX) to continuously improve planning and supplier performance.

Data model and analytics
Standardize dimensions for budget, commitment, and actuals (entity, BU, cost
center, category, supplier). Provide spend dashboards for: budget vs. actuals
vs. commitments, forecast‑to‑complete, contract utilization, early‑pay savings,
and approval lead times. Track exceptions (over‑budget, rejections, waivers) and
drill to transaction.

High - level process

 1. Define strategy and targets: Set fiscal targets by category/BU, phasing,
    reserve and contingency rules, and exception policy.
 2. Allocate and publish budgets: Distribute to owners and load approved amounts
    with dimensions and phasing.
 3. Configure controls and limits: Turn on budget control points, tolerances,
    signing limits, and workflows.
 4. Execute with control: Run requisitions/POs against budgets; apply sourcing
    thresholds; use contracts/agreements to preserve rates and capacity.
 5. Monitor performance: Review budget burn, commitments, and variances; surface
    at‑risk lines and approval bottlenecks.
 6. Manage changes: Process budget transfers and amendments; enforce
    change‑order re‑approvals; document rationale.
 7. Optimize for value: Capture early‑pay discounts, rebalance categories, and
    shift spend to preferred/diverse suppliers within policy.
 8. Review and improve: Quarterly retrospective on policy hits, cycle time, and
    savings; adjust limits, tolerances, and targets.

Roles and responsibilities

 * Chief Procurement Officer: Owns policy, targets, and exception governance;
   approves large transfers and high‑risk waivers.
 * Category Manager: Builds category budgets, monitors burn and savings, drives
   rebalancing and supplier mix.
 * Finance Controller/FP&A: Sets fiscal guardrails, approves budget
   journals/transfers, ensures accounting integrity and audit trails.
 * Procurement Operations: Configures controls, runs approval workflows, and
   maintains signing‑limit matrices.
 * Budget Owners (BU/Cost Center): Plan bottom‑up needs, approve local spend
   within limits, request in‑year transfers.
 * Treasury/AP: Aligns payment timing and cash discount policies with
   working‑capital goals.

Dynamics 365 configuration pointers

 * Budgeting and Budget Control: Define budget models, codes, cycles, and budget
   control rules at the correct dimension set; enable checks at requisition/PO.
 * Procurement policies: Enforce catalog/category access, RFQ thresholds, and
   re‑approval rules on PO changes.
 * Signing limits and workflows: Implement monetary thresholds and conditional
   logic (category, risk, prepayment) for requisitions, agreements, POs, and
   change orders.
 * Budget transfers: Use budget register entries and transfer journals with
   workflow, attachments, and effective dates.
 * Analytics: Publish Power BI reports for budget vs. actuals vs. commitments,
   approval SLA, and exception management.

Operational controls and KPIs

 * Controls: Hard/soft budget checks at PR/PO, dual approval for high‑risk, SoD
   on vendor/bank updates, documented budget‑transfer journals, quarterly policy
   review.
 * KPIs: Budget adherence %, commitment coverage %, approval cycle time, waiver
   rate, % spend under contract, early‑pay savings realized, rework due to
   change‑order rejections, exception rate (over‑budget attempts), share to
   preferred/diverse suppliers within target.

Deliverables

 * Spend Strategy Playbook (targets, phasing, sourcing thresholds).
 * Signing‑Limit Matrix and Approval Routes.
 * Budget Control and Tolerance Settings (by category/entity).
 * Budget Transfer Policy and Journal Templates.
 * Quarterly Spend Review Pack (variance bridges, actions, owners, due dates).

preferences. Require dual approval for high‑risk items (e.g., prepayments, new
vendor, non‑PO spend). Enforce Segregation of Duties so requesters cannot
approve their own spend or vendor master/bank changes. Budget transfers and
in‑year adjustments Allow controlled transfers between cost centers/categories
with: * Clear reasons (demand shift, price change, project acceleration). * Caps
(e.g., ≤10% of original budget without CFO OK). * Traceable journal entries,
effective dates, and audit trails. * A quarterly rebasing cadence to avoid
constant micro‑moves. Emergency top‑ups should be routed via a short, documented
approval path with post‑facto review. Change‑order and variance governance
Define which changes (quantity, price, schedule) require re‑approval and which
can be auto‑accepted within tolerances. Log root causes (scope change, supplier
lead time, FX) to continuously improve planning and supplier performance. Data
model and analytics Standardize dimensions for budget, commitment, and actuals
(entity, BU, cost center, category, supplier). Provide spend dashboards for:
budget vs. actuals vs. commitments, forecast‑to‑complete, contract utilization,
early‑pay savings, and approval lead times. Track exceptions (over‑budget,
rejections, waivers) and drill to transaction. High - level process 1. Define
strategy and targets: Set fiscal targets by category/BU, phasing, reserve and
contingency rules, and exception policy. 2. Allocate and publish budgets:
Distribute to owners and load approved amounts with dimensions and phasing. 3.
Configure controls and limits: Turn on budget control points, tolerances,
signing limits, and workflows. 4. Execute with control: Run requisitions/POs
against budgets; apply sourcing thresholds; use contracts/agreements to preserve
rates and capacity. 5. Monitor performance: Review budget burn, commitments, and
variances; surface at‑risk lines and approval bottlenecks. 6. Manage changes:
Process budget transfers and amendments; enforce change‑order re‑approvals;
document rationale. 7. Optimize for value: Capture early‑pay discounts,
rebalance categories, and shift spend to preferred/diverse suppliers within
policy. 8. Review and improve: Quarterly retrospective on policy hits, cycle
time, and savings; adjust limits, tolerances, and targets. Roles and
responsibilities * Chief Procurement Officer: Owns policy, targets, and
exception governance; approves large transfers and high‑risk waivers. * Category
Manager: Builds category budgets, monitors burn and savings, drives rebalancing
and supplier mix. * Finance Controller/FP&A: Sets fiscal guardrails, approves
budget journals/transfers, ensures accounting integrity and audit trails. *
Procurement Operations: Configures controls, runs approval workflows, and
maintains signing‑limit matrices. * Budget Owners (BU/Cost Center): Plan
bottom‑up needs, approve local spend within limits, request in‑year transfers. *
Treasury/AP: Aligns payment timing and cash discount policies with
working‑capital goals. Dynamics 365 configuration pointers * Budgeting and
Budget Control: Define budget models, codes, cycles, and budget control rules at
the correct dimension set; enable checks at requisition/PO. * Procurement
policies: Enforce catalog/category access, RFQ thresholds, and re‑approval rules
on PO changes. * Signing limits and workflows: Implement monetary thresholds and
conditional logic (category, risk, prepayment) for requisitions, agreements,
POs, and change orders. * Budget transfers: Use budget register entries and
transfer journals with workflow, attachments, and effective dates. * Analytics:
Publish Power BI reports for budget vs. actuals vs. commitments, approval SLA,
and exception management. Operational controls and KPIs * Controls: Hard/soft
budget checks at PR/PO, dual approval for high‑risk, SoD on vendor/bank updates,
documented budget‑transfer journals, quarterly policy review. * KPIs: Budget
adherence %, commitment coverage %, approval cycle time, waiver rate, % spend
under contract, early‑pay savings realized, rework due to change‑order
rejections, exception rate (over‑budget attempts), share to preferred/diverse
suppliers within target. Deliverables * Spend Strategy Playbook (targets,
phasing, sourcing thresholds). * Signing‑Limit Matrix and Approval Routes. *
Budget Control and Tolerance Settings (by category/entity). * Budget Transfer
Policy and Journal Templates. * Quarterly Spend Review Pack (variance bridges,
actions, owners, due dates).

procurement transactions. Signing limits are configured based on roles,
departments, or individual users, ensuring that purchase requisitions, purchase

unauthorized commitments and supporting audit requirements. Approval workflows
can be tailored to reflect complex organizational structures, with escalation
paths for exceptions and comprehensive logging of approval actions for
compliance and reporting.

Description:

provides organizations with tools to enforce budgetary discipline throughout the
procurement lifecycle. Budget control parameters can be set at various
levels—company, department, project, or cost center—and integrated with purchase
requisitions, purchase orders, and invoices. The system automatically checks
available budgets before allowing commitments, issues warnings or blocks
transactions that exceed limits, and supports flexible rules for exceptions.
Real-time reporting and dashboards enable finance and procurement teams to
monitor compliance, identify trends, and take corrective action as needed.

Description:
Analyze sourcing market builds a repeatable market‑intelligence cadence to
understand category dynamics, supplier landscape, and cost/risk drivers so you
can choose the right sourcing strategy, timing, and partners. It connects
internal demand and spend signals with external market data to inform RFx
approach, negotiation levers, contract terms, and risk posture.

Scope and objectives
Establish a disciplined view of the external market for each category, quantify
price/capacity trends and competitive intensity, identify qualified and diverse
suppliers, and translate insights into sourcing waves, award strategies, and
guardrails for negotiations. Outcomes include better timing to market, improved
price/term performance, risk‑adjusted supplier portfolios, and increased award
share to diverse and sustainable suppliers.

What to analyze

 * Market structure and capacity: supplier count/size, regional footprint,
   utilization, consolidation/M&A, entry barriers, alternate materials or
   make‑vs‑buy options.
 * Cost drivers and indices: commodities, labor, energy, logistics, FX,
   tariffs/duties; build should‑cost and index‑linked pricing constructs.
 * Competitive benchmarks: price corridors, service SLAs, lead times,
   warranty/after‑sales norms, rebate practices.
 * Risk signals: financial health, concentration, geo‑political exposure, ESG
   and regulatory compliance, cyber posture, supply chain resilience.
 * Diversity and sustainability: certified diverse suppliers, local/regional
   options, emissions and packaging standards, ethical sourcing.
 * Internal demand/spend: specification rationalization, aggregation
   opportunities, incumbent performance, quality/NCR history, total
   cost‑to‑serve.

High‑level process

 1. Baseline demand and spend: consolidate 12–24 months of demand forecasts,
    specs, and contract expirations; segment by category, region, and
    criticality.
 2. Map supplier landscape: identify incumbents, challengers, and new entrants;
    capture diversity and sustainability credentials; assess capacity and
    geographic coverage.
 3. Quantify cost drivers: align categories to external indices and FX; produce
    should‑cost models with scenario bands (base/optimistic/pessimistic).
 4. Assess risk and compliance: screen sanctions/SSPA/privacy, financial health,
    ESG attestations; rate suppliers and regions; define red‑flag thresholds.
 5. Build the sourcing thesis: decide RFx vs. direct award, single vs.
    multi‑source, global vs. regional splits; set wave plan and award heuristics
    (price/quality/risk/ESG weights).
 6. Define negotiation levers: index‑linked clauses, volume tiers, service
    credits, rebates, VMI/consignment, lead‑time commitments, dual‑sourcing
    safeguards.
 7. Prepare the market: supplier briefings and data rooms via the collaboration
    portal; finalize RFx questionnaires and scoring; publish calendar and rules.
 8. Execute RFx and analyze: run sealed bids/rounds; normalize price and
    non‑price terms against should‑cost; run sensitivity and multi‑objective
    scoring; produce award recommendation.
 9. Close loop and monitor: codify index/FX adjustment rules, service KPIs, and
    business‑event alerts in contracts; schedule quarterly market refresh and
    supplier QBRs.

Roles and responsibilities

 * Category Manager: owns thesis, wave plan, RFx content, and award
   recommendations.
 * Sourcing Analyst: builds spend cuts, market models, should‑costs, and KPI
   dashboards.
 * Risk/Compliance: runs sanctions/SSPA/privacy/ESG checks; approves exceptions.
 * Finance/FP&A: validates index/FX mechanics and TCO; aligns to budgets and
   cash targets.
 * Sustainability & Diversity: curates certified suppliers and tracks
   award/spend attainment.
 * Legal/Contracts: authors indexation, SLA, and risk‑transfer clauses; ensures
   auditability.

Dynamics 365 and Microsoft support

 * Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management: procurement categories, RFQ management,
   trade agreements, vendor performance, rebate management, vendor consigned
   inventory, change management and approvals.
 * Supplier collaboration portal: supplier onboarding, profile updates,
   certifications, document exchange, bid responses.
 * Finance: AP terms alignment (cash discounts, payment methods), positive pay,
   centralized payments, rebate settlement.
 * Microsoft Fabric/Power BI: category spend cubes, price/index trackers,
   supplier scorecards, QBR packs, and variance bridges.
 * Copilot/Agents: narrative market summaries, anomaly detection on bid
   responses, next‑best negotiation levers, auto‑drafted RFx/Q&A and award
   memos.

Operational controls

 * Policy alignment: competitive bidding thresholds, AVL enforcement, RFx
   fairness rules, confidentiality, and SoD (RFx author vs. approver vs.
   awarder).
 * Data governance: versioned RFx, sealed bids, audit trails, index sources and
   update cadence, evidence for diversity certifications.
 * Risk gates: mandatory checks for sanctions/ESG/privacy; escalation paths for
   high‑risk awards; dual‑sourcing for critical items.
 * Contractization: index‑linked pricing clauses, service credits,
   exit/transition terms, step‑in rights, and business‑event alerts (late ASN,
   OTIF breaches).

KPIs and signals to track

 * Savings vs. should‑cost and vs. prior period; index‑adjusted price variance.
 * Award share to diverse and sustainable suppliers; number of certified diverse
   suppliers invited/responding/awarded.
 * Supplier risk score trend; dual‑source coverage for critical SKUs; regional
   exposure.
 * RFx cycle time; supplier participation and compliance rates; bid
   normalization deltas.
 * Contract leakage: off‑contract spend, price/term deviations, change‑order
   incidence.
 * Service KPIs: OTIF, lead‑time adherence, quality/NCR rate, corrective action
   closure.

Deliverables

 * Category market brief and should‑cost workbook with index mapping and
   scenarios.
 * Wave plan and negotiation playbook per category.
 * RFx package (questionnaire, scoring model, data room contents).
 * Award recommendation, TCO analysis, and risk register with mitigations.
 * Contract clause library for indexation, SLAs, rebates, and sustainability.
 * Quarterly market update pack and supplier QBR deck.

Implementation tips
Start with top 5 spend categories and near‑term expirations. Normalize specs to
expand competition. Tie payment terms and early‑pay discounts to treasury
targets. Use index bands rather than fixed prices for volatile inputs. Blend
global and regional awards to hedge geopolitics and logistics. Bake supplier‑led
innovation and sustainability metrics into SLAs—and pay for performance.

scenario is designed to enhance supply chain resilience and ensure continuity of
operations through data-driven supplier management.

Description:

process in Dynamics 365 Commerce, Finance, Project Operations, and Supply Chain
Management. This process is part of the procure to pay end-to-end process. It
helps you find, select, and evaluate vendors for your business needs.




The manage vendor relationships business process area is an essential part of
the procure to pay process in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management. Dynamics 365
includes a comprehensive set of capabilities to help you streamline vendor
management. You can use it to:

 * Search for potential vendors based on product type, location, price, and
   other criteria.
 * Approve qualified vendors and create vendor records with all the relevant
   information.
 * Update vendor records as needed, such as changing bank accounts or payment
   terms.
 * Monitor vendor performance using various metrics, such as delivery time,
   quality, and compliance.
 * Collaborate with vendors through a centralized platform that shows purchase
   orders, invoices, and consignment stock.

The manage vendor relationships business process area helps you optimize your
supply chain operations and achieve better business outcomes. You should
implement it at the start of your Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management
implementation. It's a foundational process for any organization.

Description:
Develop supplier segments organizes the vendor base into meaningful groups so
procurement can target sourcing strategies, enforce policies, track supplier
diversity, and optimize buying outcomes across categories, regions, and business
units.

This process supports both portal-driven segmentation (via supplier
collaboration) and manual maintenance in the ERP, and it explicitly includes
supplier diversity attributes and purchasing demographics.

Scope and outcomes The process defines the segmentation framework, enriches
suppliers with the attributes that place them into segments, and keeps those
segments current as suppliers onboard, update certifications, or performance
shifts. Outcomes include clear segment definitions (e.g., strategic vs.
transactional), validated diversity classifications, visibility into purchasing
demographics (who buys from whom, where, and for what), and segment-specific
playbooks for sourcing, risk, and performance management.

Segmentation model (what to capture)

 * Business identity: legal entity, parent/child relationships, tax IDs,
   NAICS/industry, geography.
 * Commercial markers: category fit, price lists/trade agreements, contract
   status, capacity/lead times, delivery lanes.
 * Risk and compliance: sanctions/KYC status, insurance, sustainability/ESG
   attestations, cybersecurity posture.
 * Performance: on‑time delivery, quality metrics, responsiveness, dispute rate,
   claim history.
 * Diversity: minority‑owned, women‑owned, veteran‑owned, disability‑owned,
   LGBTQ+‑owned, small/disadvantaged business, indigenous, local/regional
   designations; certification bodies; effective/expiry dates.
 * Purchasing demographics: spend by business unit/region/cost center, category
   mix, order frequency, average PO value, tail vs. strategic spend share.

Data sources (how it gets populated)

 * Supplier collaboration portal self‑service forms for profile, certifications,
   banking, sustainability and diversity disclosures, with evidence uploads and
   dates.
 * Manual entry in system for vendor groups, classifications, category
   assignments, and policy flags when portal is not in scope.
 * Controlled imports (CSV/cXML/API) from supplier registries (e.g., diversity
   certifiers), CLM systems, and performance data from receiving/quality
   modules.

Operating model

 * Portal‑driven segmentation: suppliers submit/maintain profile and
   certifications; workflows validate and place suppliers into segments
   automatically based on rules.
 * Manual in‑system segmentation: procurement analysts assign vendor groups,
   risk scores, diversity flags, and category memberships directly in ERP when
   collaboration is unavailable or during transition.
 * Hybrid: start manual to establish baseline, then transition segments to
   portal upkeep; keep critical attributes under workflow (e.g., bank changes,
   diversity certification).

High‑level process

 1.  Define segment taxonomy and rules
     
     * Set the canonical list of segments (e.g., strategic, preferred,
       qualified, tail), diversity attributes, and risk tiers; publish the
       decision rules and data dictionary.

 2.  Configure master data and security
     
     * Create vendor groups/classes, category associations, mandatory
       attributes, and approval workflows. Set role‑based access for who can
       view/change sensitive fields.

 3.  Enable the supplier collaboration portal
     
     * Publish onboarding questionnaires, required documents, and self‑service
       profile pages for diversity, sustainability, and banking; map each field
       to ERP attributes.

 4.  Collect and validate data
     
     * Intake portal submissions and imports; validate certifications (issuer,
       number, effective/expiry), run basic KYC/sanctions checks, and flag
       missing or expired evidence.

 5.  Apply segmentation rules
     
     * Assign segment, risk tier, and diversity status based on rules (e.g.,
       spend thresholds, category fit, performance, certifications). Record
       effective dates and rationale.

 6.  Enrich with purchasing demographics
     
     * Link historic and rolling spend by BU/region/category to the supplier
       record; compute purchase frequency, order size, and tail‑spend indicators
       to refine segment placement.

 7.  Approve and publish segments
     
     * Route changes through workflow for procurement/category manager approval;
       publish segments to sourcing, requisitioning policies, and supplier
       performance dashboards.

 8.  Govern usage in downstream processes
     
     * Bind segments to policies (e.g., RFQ routing to “preferred,” auto‑blocks
       for “not qualified,” diversity‑spend targets in analytics, guided buying
       recommendations).

 9.  Monitor and refresh
     
     * Schedule reviews for expiring certifications, material performance
       shifts, M&A events; automatically notify suppliers via portal to update
       expiring documents.

 10. Improve the model
     
     * Review segment drift vs. outcomes (savings, risk incidents,
       diversity‑spend attainment); refine rules and thresholds; retire unused
       attributes.

Roles and responsibilities

 * Procurement/category manager: owns taxonomy, thresholds, and approvals;
   resolves exceptions.
 * Supplier onboarding/operations: validates submissions, runs checks, and
   manages workflows.
 * Diversity & inclusion lead (or ESG): defines accepted certification bodies
   and target reporting.
 * Risk/compliance: maintains KYC/sanctions rules, approves sensitive changes.
 * Finance/AP: verifies banking and tax data; ensures SoD and auditability.
 * Business stakeholders: supply purchasing demographics and feedback on
   supplier fit.

Dynamics 365 support

 * Vendor information management and vendor groups/classifications for segments,
   risk, and policies.
 * Supplier collaboration portal for self‑service profile maintenance,
   confirmations, and document upload.
 * Purchasing policies that reference vendor groups/segments to allow/deny
   categories or enforce RFQs.
 * Trade agreements and approved vendor list to bind segments to price/contract
   usage.
 * Analytics via Power BI/Microsoft Fabric to report diversity spend, segment
   performance, tail spend, and purchasing demographics.

Supplier diversity and purchasing demographics (practical guidance)

 * Diversity capture: model diversity as structured fields with certification
   authority, certificate ID, effective/expiry, and attach artifacts;
   differentiate self‑attested vs. certified.
 * Targets and tracking: define percentage goals (e.g., percent of addressable
   spend to certified diverse suppliers) by category and region; monitor
   progress monthly.
 * Purchasing demographics: publish a quarterly heatmap showing who buys from
   which segments by business unit and location; use it to rebalance work to
   diverse/preferred suppliers without increasing risk.
 * Guardrails: enforce evidence-on-file rules for diversity claims and
   auto‑expire designations upon certificate expiry; route reinstatement through
   validation workflow.

Operational controls and KPIs

 * Controls: maker‑checker for profile changes; workflow approvals for
   risk/diversity flags; automated reminders for expiring certifications; audit
   trails for attribute changes.
 * KPIs: percent of spend through preferred/strategic segments; diverse‑supplier
   spend attainment; number of active diverse suppliers by category/region;
   average time to validate new supplier; share of tail spend; policy violations
   avoided; data completeness score for vendor profiles.

Deliverables

 * Segmentation taxonomy and data dictionary.
 * Configured vendor groups/classifications and workflows.
 * Onboarding questionnaires and document lists (portal).
 * Diversity certification playbook and accepted issuers list.
 * Dashboards: diversity spend, purchasing demographics, segment performance.

Description:
This process governs the onboarding of new suppliers following successful
application approval. It ensures vendors are properly qualified, set up in the
system, and ready for transactional engagement. It includes account creation,
contact and banking details setup, vendor demographic enrichment, legal entity
replication, and qualification workflows.

Scope and Outcomes

 * Converts approved applications into vendor accounts
 * Captures and validates supplier contact and banking details
 * Copies vendor profiles across legal entities
 * Maintains and updates vendor demographics
 * Qualifies suppliers for sourcing and purchasing
 * Outcomes include active vendor records, validated banking and tax data,
   enriched demographics, and qualified sourcing-ready suppliers

Onboarding Model

Business Identity
Legal name, registration details, tax IDs, NAICS codes, geography, parent/child
relationships

Contact Information
Primary contacts, email, phone, address, role-based access

Banking Details
Bank name, account number, routing code, currency, country, verification status

Demographics
Industry, category fit, delivery lanes, capacity, lead times

Compliance
Insurance, ESG attestations, cybersecurity posture, sanctions/KYC status

Certifications
Diversity, quality, environmental credentials, effective/expiry dates

Performance History
If applicable, includes legacy data on delivery, quality, responsiveness

Legal Entity Replication
Copy vendor records to other legal entities with mapped attributes and controls

Data Sources

 * Supplier collaboration portal: onboarding forms, document uploads,
   certifications
 * Manual entry: ERP-based vendor setup for non-portal suppliers
 * Controlled imports: CSV, cXML, API from registries, certifiers, CLM systems
 * Performance data: receiving, quality, and finance modules

Operating Model

 * Portal-driven onboarding: suppliers submit profiles, documents,
   certifications
 * Manual onboarding: procurement teams create vendor records directly in ERP
 * Hybrid: initial manual setup followed by portal-based updates and maintenance

High-Level Process

 1. Approve Application
    Validate supplier application and convert to vendor record

 2. Create Vendor Account
    Generate vendor ID, assign vendor group, set up legal entity associations

 3. Capture Contact and Banking Details
    Enter and verify contact info, banking data, tax details

 4. Enrich Vendor Profile
    Add demographics, certifications, compliance attributes

 5. Replicate Across Legal Entities
    Copy vendor data to relevant entities with mapped fields and controls

 6. Qualify Vendor
    Assign category memberships, risk scores, diversity flags

 7. Publish Vendor Record
    Make vendor available for sourcing, RFQs, purchasing

 8. Monitor and Maintain
    Schedule reviews for expiring certifications, update profiles, notify
    suppliers

Roles and Responsibilities

 * Procurement/category manager: owns onboarding criteria, approvals, vendor
   group assignments
 * Supplier onboarding operations: validates submissions, manages workflows
 * Risk/compliance: maintains KYC/sanctions rules, approves sensitive changes
 * Diversity & inclusion lead: defines certification bodies, reporting targets
 * Finance/AP: verifies banking and tax data, ensures SoD and auditability
 * Business stakeholders: provide feedback on supplier fit and purchasing needs

Dynamics 365 Support

 * Vendor information management: vendor groups, classifications, segments
 * Supplier collaboration portal: self-service onboarding, document uploads
 * Workflow automation: approvals, validations, notifications
 * Purchasing policies: enforce sourcing rules, RFQ eligibility
 * Analytics: dashboards for onboarding throughput, diversity attainment, vendor
   performance

Deliverables

 * Configured vendor groups, classifications, workflows
 * Onboarding questionnaires, document lists
 * Diversity certification playbook, accepted issuers list
 * Dashboards: onboarding metrics, diversity spend, vendor performance

Title 5: Maintain vendors in Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management
Description:
Manually create a vendor record. When you create a vendor account, you enter
information about the vendor. This information is used to automatically enter
data in documents and to track activity that involves the vendor. For example,
you can configure the following information for a vendor: Assign a vendor group.
Every vendor must be assigned to a vendor group. The vendors in a vendor group
have parameters that they share. For example, they might have the same terms of
payment. Configure the vendor for catalog import. Vendors can provide a file
that contains the catalog of their items and services. This file can be uploaded
so that your workers can order from the vendor. Assign the vendor to procurement
categories. Allow an existing vendor to do business with another legal entity in
your organization. Put a vendor on hold for specific types of transactions. Set
up banking information for the vendor, so that you can send payments
electronically. Set up tax, delivery, invoice, and payment information for the
vendor. By default, these settings are copied to new documents that you create
for the vendor. Set up default financial dimensions that are used to
automatically post transactions with the vendor to financial accounts. To speed
up the process of creating vendor accounts, you can create templates. To create
a template, on the Vendor page, on the Action Pane, select Options > Record
info. Then select Company accounts template. Company account templates are
shared with other users. You can also create a user template for your own use.
You can't delete a vendor that is associated with other records, such as
contacts or products
